title: 4 Jedi Mind Tricks for Avoiding Burnout
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that lasting impact in teaching depends on tending the teacher's own heart and mind, which he likens to a garden that decays if left on autopilot. He starts from the premise that nobody enters teaching hoping to burn out, so scorning burnt-out veterans is both unfair and a seed of the same rot. He then offers four mental habits: separate your worth from your job performance, treat failure as learning, aim at students' good rather than their approval, and let hardship build your character. A story about a disengaged student named Belle shows how honesty rooted in concern earned more trust than flattery would have. The piece is a career-sustainability argument for the profession side of teaching.
points: Tying identity to job performance wrecks teachers in both directions: success breeds pride and dependence, failure breeds shame and cynicism.
Reframing each classroom failure as someone getting smarter (the teacher) turned his worst student-teaching days into his most productive ones.
Seeking students' good over their approval makes tough, honest conversations possible, and it paradoxically earned him more respect.
Teachers should visibly pursue the character strengths they hope students will grow, treating hard seasons as a furnace for their own character.
quotes: So here’s what few teacher books will tell you — great teaching is only possible when your heart is in it, and yet there are so many factors seemingly bent on removing our hearts completely. Back when I started this blog, I considered standards one more group of things that were out to “get” us teachers, to rip out the heart of our profession.

As a new teacher, I used to look down on older, burnt out teachers until I realized that none of them, years ago with newly minted teaching certificates in their hands, dreamed of one day becoming burnt out gripemasters.
When your job performance is linked, inside your head and heart, to your worth as a person, success will affect you like a narcotic. You will become proud; you will think you’re super-amazing.

I went from the guy who fails mopingly to the guy who fails excitedly because of the lessons I was learning. It turned my worst days into some of my most productive; days in which my greatest weaknesses were laid bare like those nightmares where you realized you’re not wearing pants became days in which my strength as a teacher grew the most.

My goal is not to be the messiah of my students — it is to impact them. For the rest of the year, I was able to use my increased influence with Belle to help her grow in her literacy skills, simply because I made the right call in the tough situation.

I’m not saying be a jerk to kids — I am saying you’ve got to have higher goals than to simply have them love you. Interestingly enough, since I’ve started to embrace this, I’ve found that I am more liked by students, not less.
